Biotin (Vitamin H or
B7)
AI: 30 mg
Peptidyl biocytin
Biotin acts as a cofactor
for biotin-dependent
carboxylases that
play critical roles in
the intermediate
metabolism of
gluconeogenesis,
fatty acid synthesis,
and amino acid
catabolism.
Biotin catalyzes the transfer of
CO2 groups to various target
macromolecules. Biotin
comprises a ureido ring,
a tetrahydrothiophene ring, and
a valeric acid side chain. It is the
ureido ring that functions as the
CO2 carrier. The overall reaction
of biotin consists of two steps.
In the ﬁrst step, carboxy-
phosphate is generated from
bicarbonate with MgATP as an
energy source. In the second
step, carboxy-biotin results
from the nucleophilic attack of
the carboxy-phosphate
intermediate’s carboxyl group.
The enzyme-biotin CO2 is then
transferred to an appropriate
receptor.
Biotinidase deﬁciency,
a rare inherited
disorder, is the most
common cause of
biotin deﬁciency.
Biotinidase.
Biotinidase catalyzes
the conversion of
biocytin to biotin.
